title: Stop, stabilize, signal

action.text: Pause on stable ground and check the scene before approaching an injured person. Check responsiveness, breathing and obvious life-threatening injury.
If someone is unresponsive, breathing abnormally or bleeding severely, call 911 and follow the dispatcher. Give your location and the immediate hazard.
If travel has stopped, use available shelter and insulation. Tell everyone where to wait and who is trying to make contact.

stop.text: Leave immediate danger by a clearly safer path. If location and safe travel are uncertain, stay findable and seek help.

title: Assess before you move

action.text: Inventory the group, the weather, the remaining daylight and the last place you can identify confidently.
Compare what you see with a mapped trail, junction or other reliable feature. Record the last verified place if your current location is uncertain.
Move only when the group can name a safe next checkpoint and is able to reach it. Keep current conditions and the slowest member in the decision.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Use location, daylight and group condition to decide whether travel makes sense.
applies: A stopped group with a potentially safe route and enough time to assess.
equipment: Offline map or paper map, watch, light and weather information if available.

verify.text: Before stepping off, someone can point to the next checkpoint and explain how the party will know it has reached it.

stop.text: Weather, terrain or group condition can invalidate a previously reasonable route. Halt if the next checkpoint becomes uncertain.

diagram: Last verified place | Check group and conditions | Name a safe next point

title: Stay, signal or move

action.text: Stop. If an immediate hazard threatens the spot, reach safer ground nearby only when you can identify a safe way there.
Contact 911 when help is needed and service is available. Report last known position, landmarks, number of people, injuries and any planned movement.
If you cannot determine a safe route, stay together in a findable location, shelter from weather and prepare to signal when responders are nearby.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Make an explicit choice between staying findable and moving to a known safe position.
applies: Lost or overdue outdoor party. Immediate danger and known route are separate questions.
equipment: Phone or emergency communicator, whistle, light, bright material and weather protection if available.

verify.text: Your location description gives responders a usable starting point. Mark a plan change in your message if you must move.

stop.text: Never attempt an uncertain shortcut over water or ice to reach a signal or a road.

diagram: Immediate danger? | Safe route known? | If uncertain, stay findable

title: Leave a usable trip plan
origin: B014 reconstruction R01 and B012 P02

action.text: Record the starting point, planned route and return time. Include names or party size and expected vehicle location if relevant.
Give the plan to a trusted contact and agree on the overdue reporting point and what information to pass to responders.
Carry a copy and notify the contact of significant changes when you can. Check back in at return.

equipment: Paper plan or saved message, mapped route, and contact information.

verify.text: Your contact can identify the trailhead and say when they should act.

stop.text: If nobody can act on an overdue report, reconsider the route and exposure before departing.

title: Pack by failure mode
origin: NPS Ten Essentials; new manuscript

action.text: Map darkness, navigation loss, exposure and delayed return to independent kit functions. Consider Sun protection and repair supplies as conditions warrant.
Check each function at home: a light turns on, the map works offline, the shelter can be set up, and spare insulation is dry.
Give shared gear an owner. Ensure the group can reach critical pieces without emptying all the packs.

verify.text: Simulate one failure and retrieve the correct item without a signal or a search through loose gear.

stop.text: Narrow or postpone the trip if critical protection or navigation is absent.

title: Set a turnaround before departure
origin: B014 P18 and B012 P02

action.text: Identify a decision point and latest turnaround time. Build in daylight and delay margin for the slowest group member.
At each reliable checkpoint compare actual progress and conditions with the plan. Recalculate when the return route or pace changes.
Turn back early if visibility, access, group condition or the return margin deteriorates and the return route is known safe.

verify.text: The group can name the trigger and the place where it will reassess.

title: Give rescuers a usable location
origin: B013 P13 and B014 P16

action.text: Give the site or park name plus trailhead, road, junction or other verified landmark. If sending coordinates, read the format shown by the device.
State how many people are involved, whether anyone is injured and what nearby hazards affect access.
Specify whether you will wait or must move. Follow dispatcher directions and communicate changes if you can.

equipment: Phone or suitable communicator, offline map and light if available.

verify.text: Ask whether your location was received and which approach the responder wants you to use, if any.

title: Keep track of everyone
origin: NPS Hike Smart and B014 P17

action.text: Choose a route and pace that the whole group can manage. Agree that nobody leaves a junction before the group is accounted for.
Check attendance at the start, at junctions and before leaving a long stop. Give the back of the group a way to signal the front.
If someone is missing, keep the remaining group together. Record the last place and time where the person was seen and contact responders when needed.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent unplanned separation before it becomes a search.
applies: Group travel on land in uneven terrain, variable visibility or busy trail networks.
equipment: Group roster or head count, paper or offline map and an agreed signal.

verify.text: Everyone knows the next checkpoint and the count agrees at every major stop.

stop.text: Avoid splitting into an uncoordinated search. Follow directions from responders.

title: Prepare a communication backup
origin: NPS Ten Essentials and B014 P15/P16

action.text: Save the route, emergency numbers and trip information before leaving coverage. Carry a paper copy independent of the phone battery.
Check how your equipment works before the trip and agree on an overdue trigger with a contact. A signal device helps nearby responders but cannot promise that someone knows your location.
If no message can get through, avoid uncertain travel just to find signal. Prepare to be located using known landmarks, shelter and available signals.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending

applies: Trips without dependable voice or data service.
equipment: Phone, paper map and trip plan, whistle and light. Add a suitable emergency communicator if available.

verify.text: Demonstrate one location report and one backup signal while the phone is disconnected.

stop.text: Do not assume help has been dispatched if you cannot confirm that a message was received.

title: Recognize the moment to call for help
origin: American Red Cross first aid; new manuscript

action.text: Look for ongoing danger before approaching. Observe responsiveness, breathing and life-threatening bleeding.
Call 911 for unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing or life-threatening bleeding. Give the exact location and describe what you see in plain language.
Follow the dispatcher and work within your training. If someone else is available, assign them to communicate and guide responders.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize emergency signs and transfer clear information to EMS.
applies: Lay responder at a sudden injury or illness in the United States.
equipment: Phone or emergency communicator and first-aid equipment as available.

verify.text: State the emergency, location and access route. Confirm which person is calling.

stop.text: If the scene is unsafe, keep clear and give responders the hazard details.

title: Stop at uncertain ice

action.text: Stop on stable land. Ice varies across one body of water; appearance, footsteps or a nearby measurement cannot establish your crossing.
Use a verified land route if conditions and group ability allow. If you cannot identify one, reassess time, exposure and communication from stable ground.
Share your location and the changed route or hold decision. Keep the group off the uncertain surface.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Preserve a safe land route when a winter shortcut is unverified.
applies: A walking party approaching a frozen lake, stream, flooded path or marsh.
equipment: Map and sufficient insulation and time for a safe alternative.

verify.text: The next segment stays on known ground and the group can describe its return option.

stop.text: An unverified shortcut, bridge approach or ice edge remains a stop point.

diagram: Stop on land | Identify a verified land option | Hold and seek help if uncertain

title: Turn back at a flooded route
origin: FEMA flood guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Turn around before entering floodwater. Its depth and force may be difficult to judge and the road surface can be damaged.
Check local evacuation instructions and choose an official, open alternate route or safe higher location. Avoid relying on a previous crossing or another vehicle's tracks.
Report your updated position and route to the appropriate contact when you can. Call for emergency help if trapped.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Preserve an evacuation option when a familiar road or foot route floods.
applies: Rising or standing floodwater blocking a road, path or crossing.
equipment: Current emergency directions and a map for alternatives if available.

verify.text: A safe route is confirmed from reliable local information, or the group is waiting at a safer location.

stop.text: Do not drive or walk around a closure into floodwater.

diagram: Flooded road ahead | Turn around early | Use official route or higher ground
visual: Road closure is a stop condition, independent of the apparent depth.

title: Assess route, weather and group risk before departure
origin: MN DNR, NPS Hike Smart and NWS alerts; new manuscript

action.text: Review forecast temperatures, wind, precipitation, fire restrictions and any active Watches or Warnings for the exact route and elevation.
Match distance, elevation gain, terrain hazards and available daylight to the least experienced or slowest person in the group.
Identify bailout exits, water access and shelter points along the route, and define conditions that cancel or shorten the trip before departing.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Screen weather, terrain, daylight and group capability before committing to a route.
applies: Pre-departure planning for day or overnight outdoor travel across seasons. Conditions change rapidly and require re-checking at the trailhead.
equipment: Current forecast and alerts, topographic or trail map, daylight table and group health summary.

failure.text: Proceeding with an outdated forecast, overestimating daylight or assuming the group will speed up on unfamiliar terrain.

verify.text: Every participant can state the route length, expected return time, top weather hazard and pre-agreed cancellation trigger.

stop.text: Active Severe Weather Warnings, unresolved hazard closures or missing essential protection require postponing or changing the route.

title: Inspect critical gear before failure occurs
origin: NPS Ten Essentials and Ready.gov kit maintenance; new manuscript

action.text: Test lighting, communication devices and weather radio under battery power alone, and confirm offline maps open with airplane mode enabled.
Inspect shelter seams, poles, zippers, water containers, filter seals and first-aid expiration dates for wear, brittleness or missing parts.
Confirm cold-sensitive items such as batteries, fuel canisters and wet filters have thermal protection suited to forecast lows.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Detect degraded batteries, leaks, tears and expired supplies before entering the field.
applies: Routine pre-trip readiness check for backcountry packs and household emergency go-bags. Does not replace manufacturer servicing.

failure.text: Discovering dead batteries, cracked water lids, missing tent poles or dried-out bandages only after stopping in poor weather.

verify.text: Every life-safety subsystem passes a live hands-on function test at home and is repacked in an accessible order.

stop.text: Replace or repair damaged shelter, navigation, light or water gear before departure, or cancel the outing until functional gear is ready.

title: Assign group roles and pacing boundaries
origin: NPS Hike Smart and Ready.gov planning; new manuscript

action.text: Designate a lead who sets a sustainable pace, a sweep who stays behind the last person, and a backup navigator carrying an independent map.
Establish mandatory regroup points at every trail junction, water crossing, steep climb and visibility drop before stepping off.
Rotate check-ins for hydration, warmth, foot comfort and morale so quieter or fatigued members can call a halt without social pressure.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Maintain clear leadership, head counts and mutual accountability during group travel or emergencies.
applies: Groups of two or more hikers, families or mixed-ability parties on land. Solo travelers use external check-in contacts instead.
equipment: Written group roster, agreed whistle signals, map copy for more than one person and shared emergency contact sheet.

failure.text: Unassigned leadership, fast walkers outpacing slower members past forks, or hidden fatigue going unreported until collapse.

verify.text: Every member knows who is lead, who is sweep, what whistle signal means stop and where the next regroup point lies.

stop.text: If the group loses visual or voice accountability or someone cannot sustain the pace safely, halt immediately, regroup and revise the objective.

title: Layer alert receivers and emergency messages
origin: Ready.gov alerts, plan and NOAA Weather Radio; new manuscript

action.text: Enable Wireless Emergency Alerts and local agency notifications, and carry a battery or hand-crank NOAA Weather Radio tested for local VHF reception.
Record an out-of-area contact, local meeting points and critical medical notes on waterproof paper so communication survives a dead phone.
Prefer short text messages over voice calls during network congestion, and conserve device battery by using low-power or airplane mode between checks.

applies: Home preparedness and outdoor travel across areas with patchy cellular service or power outages.
equipment: Mobile phone with alerts enabled, battery or hand-crank NOAA Weather Radio, paper contact card and optional satellite communicator.

failure.text: Relying solely on a single smartphone battery or live data connection in a valley, storm or regional tower outage.

verify.text: Confirm NOAA Weather Radio receives the local broadcast and that every group member carries the written contact and meeting-point card.

stop.text: Never assume an unsent or unacknowledged message has triggered rescue; shift to stay-put visibility and physical signaling if contact fails.

title: Act on weather watches, warnings and abort triggers
origin: NWS flood, thunderstorm and Ready.gov evacuation guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Treat a Weather Watch as a trigger to review exits, shorten exposed routes and verify shelter options while conditions are still favorable.
Treat a Weather Warning, approaching thunder, rising runoff or rapid visibility loss as an immediate action threshold to seek proper shelter or evacuate.
Combine official alerts with on-site red flags—sudden wind shifts, darkening outflow clouds, dropping temperatures or declining group judgment—to abort early.

objective: Translate forecast alert tiers and field observations into timely stop, shelter or retreat actions.
applies: Outdoor travel and household emergency monitoring under changing storm, flood, wind, cold or wildfire conditions.
equipment: Weather alert receiver, local map showing exits and shelters, watch and written group turnaround limits.

failure.text: Waiting for rain or debris to strike before leaving a ridge, creek bed or exposed trail, or confusing a Watch with routine weather.

verify.text: The group can state the exact threshold that shifts the plan from continue to shorten, shelter or evacuate.

stop.text: When an active Warning or deteriorating field condition outpaces your return route, stop advancing and commit immediately to the safest reachable refuge.

title: Build an accessible emergency and evacuation plan
origin: Ready.gov People with Disabilities; new manuscript

action.text: Build a personal support network of at least three trusted contacts who know your plan, supply locations, mobility aids and communication preferences.
Arrange accessible evacuation transportation ahead of time and check whether local emergency management offers voluntary registries or utility priority-restoration lists.
Pack a go-bag and shelter-in-place kit with written prescriptions, device specs, backup power, spare eyewear or hearing batteries and service-animal food and water.

objective: Account for mobility, sensory, medical, power and service-animal needs before an emergency disrupts daily support.
applies: Individuals and groups with disabilities, chronic medical conditions, older adults or temporary mobility limits in home or travel settings.
equipment: Personal support network list, medication and dosage card, backup power or spare batteries, accessible transport contacts and service-animal supplies.

failure.text: Assuming standard evacuation shelters, public buses or unassisted foot routes can accommodate wheelchairs, oxygen concentrators, deaf/blind alerting or service animals.

verify.text: Review and rehearse the plan with your support network, confirming backup power duration and two accessible exit routes from home or camp.

title: Stabilize an unexpected overnight or multi-day delay
origin: NWS winter, NPS Ten Essentials and Ready.gov kit; new manuscript

action.text: Stop travel well before dark while energy and judgment remain intact, selecting a safe, dry, sheltered position clear of flood, tree and traffic hazards.
Establish immediate exposure control—wind barrier, dry ground insulation and dry rest layers—before spending effort on secondary tasks.
Inventory safe water, food, battery charge and medication across expected delay hours, assigning scheduled check-ins and conserving energy and heat.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Shift from travel mode to sustained shelter, hydration, warmth and accountability during an unplanned night or prolonged emergency.
applies: Stranded travelers, overdue hikers or households facing multi-day disruption where immediate rescue or restoration is delayed.
equipment: Shelter and ground insulation, dry spare layers, safe water supply, lighting, communication device and emergency food.

failure.text: Pushing into darkness until exhausted, neglecting ground insulation until shivering begins, or draining phone batteries on futile searches for signal.

verify.text: Every occupant has wind/ground protection, reachable exit lighting, a rationed water plan and a scheduled communication or signaling window.

stop.text: Worsening confusion, hypothermia, heat stroke, severe dehydration or an unsafe shelter site requires immediate escalation to emergency services.

title: Decide early when storm or wildfire threatens the route
origin: NWS wildfire, thunderstorm and Ready.gov evacuation; new manuscript

action.text: Monitor wind direction, smoke plumes, storm outflow gusts and official evacuation notices to keep at least two exit paths open away from the hazard.
Evacuate early along open official routes when wildfire approaches or Red Flag winds threaten your corridor; do not wait for flames or roadblocks.
If a severe thunderstorm or tornado warning intercepts you, abandon tents and exposed timber immediately for the lowest interior room of a sturdy building or hard-topped vehicle for lightning.

objective: Choose timely exit routes and hazard-specific refuge when severe storms or wildfire develop near camp or travel corridors.
applies: Outdoor travel or rural camp exposed to approaching severe thunderstorms, straight-line winds, tornado warnings or wildfire smoke and spread.
equipment: Official alert receiver, map showing multiple road or trail exits, respiratory/eye protection if smoke is present and vehicle or go-bag.

failure.text: Waiting to pack nonessential camp gear while smoke thickens, wind topples trees or a single exit road closes behind the party.

verify.text: Everyone knows the immediate departure trigger, which gear is left behind if ordered out and the designated safe rally destination.

stop.text: Never drive or walk through active flames, downed power lines, flooded crossings or zero-visibility smoke; follow emergency responder directions immediately.

title: Adapt the plan when a companion cannot keep pace
origin: NPS Hike Smart, ARC first aid and NPS emergency plan; new manuscript

action.text: Stop the entire group on safe ground and screen the slowed person for life-threatening distress, confusion, slurred speech, chest pain, hypothermia or heat stroke.
If no urgent red flags are present, rest in shelter, address footwear, hydration, nutrition and pack load redistribution, and reassess honestly.
Shorten the route to the nearest safe exit if recovery is incomplete; never leave an impaired or exhausted member alone to catch up later.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Distinguish manageable fatigue from medical distress and safely shorten, stabilize or escalate the trip.
applies: Any group outing where one participant slows sharply, develops pain or injury, or shows early signs of cold, heat or altitude illness.
equipment: First-aid kit, spare layers, safe water, communication device and offline map showing nearest bailout exits.

failure.text: Splitting the group so faster members push to the summit while a fatigued or confused companion falls behind unobserved.

verify.text: The affected person speaks clearly, moves steadily after rest and agrees with the revised exit or hold plan.

stop.text: Confusion, stumbling, inability to bear weight, severe pain, heat stroke or hypothermia requires stopping travel immediately and activating 911 or SAR.

title: Recognize and recover from core gear failure
origin: NPS Ten Essentials, CDC filter limits and Ready.gov kit; new manuscript

action.text: Watch for early failure cues—dimming headlamp, phone battery drop in cold, frozen water filter, jammed stove valve or torn shelter anchor.
Pause on safe ground and switch immediately to your independent backup system rather than improvising hazardous repairs under stress.
Recalculate your safety margin once a primary system fails; a trip relying on its last backup is a cue to turn back or stabilize early.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Spot silent or sudden failure of lighting, navigation, water treatment or shelter gear and shift safely to backups.
applies: Field travel or home emergencies when primary equipment breaks, freezes, leaks or loses power.
equipment: Redundant core gear (backup light, paper map, secondary water method, repair tape and emergency shelter).

failure.text: Continuing deeper into remote terrain after losing primary light, offline navigation, shelter integrity or water treatment without a working backup.

verify.text: Confirm the backup system functions cleanly right now and that the revised route matches your remaining safety margin.

stop.text: When both primary and backup systems for warmth, shelter, navigation or water fail, halt onward travel, protect the group and seek assistance.

title: Reject unsafe shelter sites

action.text: Check land rules and choose an established or designated site when required. Inspect the site and access route before unpacking.
Leave stream channels, low ground that can flood and other routes concentrating runoff. Upstream rain can reach a site even when the local sky is clear.
Scan overhead and upslope. Leave any spot where loose limbs, loose material or an unstable slope threaten the group.

objective: Rule out unsafe sites before judging comfort or convenience.
applies: Choosing temporary cover or a permitted campsite on land. Site rules and local hazards vary.
equipment: Map and weather information if available. Use daylight for inspection where possible.

verify.text: Identify an exit to safer ground and a place for the party away from overhead hazards and drainage paths.

stop.text: Reject a site if you cannot confirm a clear exit or if runoff, wind or falling material threatens it.

title: Block wind before building a roof

action.text: Choose the sheltered side of an existing stable barrier. Check that you remain clear of runoff and falling material.
Keep the exit easy to reach. Put on dry layers and protect yourself from the ground while conditions allow.
Reassess as wind direction or drifting changes. Seek a safer shelter if the barrier no longer works.

equipment: Existing wind barrier, insulating layers and optional shelter material made for outdoor use.

verify.text: Group members can move out without climbing over a barrier. Clothing and bedding are staying dry.

title: Make a dry insulated bed

action.text: Select ground away from runoff and above standing water. Keep dry gear out of splash and wet snow.
Place dry insulation between body and ground. Add dry layers above and keep protection available for wind and precipitation.
Check for gaps under the body and wet material after settling. Replace wet insulation or move if the site is deteriorating.

equipment: Camping pad or other dry insulating layer, dry clothing and weather cover if available.

verify.text: The body is separated from cold ground and the bedding stays dry where the person rests.

action.text: Pick a legal durable site outside runoff channels and clear of overhead hazards. Check the immediate weather before setting up.
Assemble the shelter according to its instructions. Keep exits and equipment access clear and avoid putting wet gear on dry bedding.
Inspect all attachment points and observe how the shelter responds to wind. Adjust within manufacturer limits or relocate to suitable shelter.

title: Leave a drainage channel early
origin: B012 P09 and agency flood guide

action.text: Look for connected low ground and a clear route to higher ground. Study upstream conditions as part of the decision.
Select a higher, stable site away from streambeds and gullies. Be ready to move if warnings, rising water or new runoff appear.
Leave early by a safe route to higher ground. Follow local emergency directions.

objective: Recognize where moving water will concentrate before precipitation reaches the site.
applies: Campsites and travel near creeks, gullies, marsh edges and valley bottoms.
equipment: Map, weather alerts and a light if available.

title: Seek lightning-safe shelter
origin: NWS lightning guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Plan a way to reach a substantial building or enclosed hard-topped vehicle before storms develop.
At thunder, stop outdoor activity and get to the identified shelter if safely accessible. A fabric shelter, open pavilion or isolated tree cannot provide comparable protection.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before returning outside. Reassess other hazards before departure.

title: Keep insulation dry across a stop

action.text: Adjust layers before heavy exertion and use ventilation where weather permits. Avoid getting clothing wet with sweat.
Before a stop, find wind protection and add the reserved dry layer. Separate wet items from dry insulation.
Check companions for unusual fumbles, slurred speech or confusion as exposure continues.

title: Choose shade and reduce exertion
origin: CDC heat guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Schedule exertion for cooler periods where possible. Use a shaded or air-conditioned rest location and take breaks before anyone becomes ill.
Keep safe water accessible and check the group for changes in coordination, speech or behavior.
If heat stroke is suspected, call 911 and start cooling promptly while following emergency directions.

title: Inspect a shelter after the weather changes
origin: B012 P18 and B003 shelter troubleshooting

action.text: From a safe position look for new runoff, pooling, drift at exits or displacement of the shelter and its anchors.
Keep exits free of gear or snow. Follow the shelter's operating instructions for its vents and supports. Keep combustion outside.
If you cannot restore safe conditions without remaining in danger, leave to a known safer location while the route is available.

title: Keep sleeping gear out of runoff
origin: B003 tarp and B012 shelter plates

action.text: Choose ground with no active runoff crossing the sleeping area. Consider where water will drip from the shelter and where it will flow.
Install the shelter and ground protection as instructed. Keep bedding away from standing water and wet gear.
Observe the outside drainage from a safe position after rain starts. Relocate if it starts to cross the floor or exit route.

title: Look up before stopping below trees
origin: Forest Service hazard tree guide; new manuscript

action.text: Scan for dead, damaged or leaning trees and material overhead before entering the potential fall zone.
Choose a durable site away from hazardous trees. Tell campground staff about a hazard in a designated site.
Reassess when wind rises or debris falls. Move to safer ground rather than trying to correct an unstable tree or branch.

title: Use a stranded vehicle as shelter
origin: NWS winter storm guidance; new manuscript

action.text: If no safe nearby destination is obvious, stay with the vehicle. Report your location, vehicle and people to emergency services or your contact.
Use available dry insulation and make the vehicle visible without exposing yourself to traffic or the storm.
Keep the group together and reassess if the vehicle location becomes dangerous. Follow responder directions.

title: Match shelter class to weather, terrain and group needs
origin: NPS camping gear and Ready.gov shelter; new manuscript

action.text: Compare expected low temperatures, wind exposure, rain or snow loading and insect pressure against the shelter's stated seasonal rating and floor area.
Verify that every group member can enter, exit and reach dry insulation easily, accounting for height, mobility limits and gear storage needs.
Treat lightweight tarps and emergency bivies as limited weather barriers that require skillful site selection and dry ground insulation rather than all-weather enclosures.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Select a shelter category suited to forecast wind, precipitation, low temperature and occupant mobility before departure.

failure.text: Carrying a summer mesh tent or thin foil blanket into forecast freezing rain, high winds or open alpine exposure.

verify.text: Confirm the chosen shelter matches forecast weather, fits all occupants with dry bedding and has been pitched in a dry rehearsal.

title: Choose durable legal surfaces without trenching or cutting live trees
origin: NPS Leave No Trace and USFS camping; new manuscript

action.text: Check unit camping rules and pitch on established sites, bare mineral soil, rock, gravel, dry grass or deep snow where permitted.
Rely on natural elevated topography for drainage rather than digging trenches around tents, which damages soil, violates park rules and still fails in heavy runoff.
Avoid cutting live branches, peeling bark or clearing meadow vegetation for improvised beds or poles unless facing a genuine life-safety emergency with no alternative.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Select natural high-and-dry camp pads that shed water without illegal terrain alteration or vegetation damage.
applies: Developed campgrounds and dispersed public-land campsites in forests, prairies and backcountry corridors.
equipment: Local land-agency rules, map and durable groundsheet sized to the shelter footprint.

failure.text: Pitching in a soft shoreline depression and digging a drainage ditch that floods anyway while damaging fragile banks.

verify.text: Confirm site legality, natural outward drainage slope and intact surrounding ground and live vegetation.

stop.text: Move to a permitted, naturally drained durable surface whenever site legality, drainage or surface stability is uncertain.

title: Read cold-air drainage, valley fog and frost-pocket microclimates
origin: NWS cold weather and NPS campsite selection; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that cooler, denser air flows downhill at dusk and settles in closed basins, valley bottoms and marsh margins—often producing lower temperatures and heavier frost than nearby mid-slopes.
Prefer a gently elevated, sheltered bench slightly above the valley floor—avoiding both the cold damp hollow below and the high wind-swept ridge crest above.
Keep extra dry insulation accessible because rapid radiative cooling after sunset can push cool humid hollows toward hypothermia conditions above freezing.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Avoid overnight temperature drops and heavy dew/frost caused by dense cold air pooling in terrain depressions.
applies: Clear calm nights in hilly, forested or river-valley terrain during spring, autumn and winter.
equipment: Topographic map, thermometer or forecast and dry insulating sleep system.

failure.text: Camping beside a misty creek bottom for convenience and waking soaked with heavy condensation in temperatures far colder than the forecast.

verify.text: Confirm the selected camp sits above obvious cold-air hollows and out of exposed hilltop wind corridors.

stop.text: Relocate to higher dry ground or add insulation promptly if valley fog, pooling chill or sudden frost threatens sleeping gear dryness.

diagram: Cold air sinks into hollow | Exposed ridge catches wind | Choose sheltered mid-slope bench

title: Screen slopes for avalanche terrain, cornices and runout zones
origin: National Avalanche Center and USFS avalanche guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Check official regional avalanche forecasts before travel and treat slopes roughly 30 to 45 degrees—and terrain directly beneath them—as avalanche hazard zones.
Look far upslope above flat valley bottoms and meadows; large slides travel well beyond steep ground into seemingly gentle runout paths and gullies.
Avoid overhanging wind-sculpted snow cornices along ridge crests and stay clear of steep snow-loaded gullies or recent debris piles when stopping or camping.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Exclude avalanche start zones, gullies and flat runout paths before selecting any winter rest stop or camp.
applies: Snow-covered hilly, bluff or mountain terrain during winter and spring thaw.
equipment: Regional avalanche forecast where published, topographic slope map and winter navigation tools.

failure.text: Pitching a winter tent on a flat valley floor directly under an unassessed steep snow slope or overhanging cornice.

verify.text: Confirm the site sits clear of steep upper slopes, overhead cornices and connected gully runout paths using both terrain inspection and map contours.

stop.text: Without formal avalanche training, rescue gear and favorable current forecasts, exclude all avalanche slopes and runout zones completely.

diagram: Steep 30-45 deg start zone | Flat runout path below | Camp outside connected paths
visual: Environmental slope profile separating steep avalanche start zones, overhanging cornices, valley runout reach and excluded camp boundaries. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Assess rockfall zones, cliff bases and saturated hillsides
origin: NPS campsite selection and USFS hazard guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Scan above the site for fractured cliff faces, loose boulders perched on soil, fresh rock debris at the base and leaning trees rooted in shallow wet earth.
Recognize that freeze-thaw mornings, heavy rainfall, root saturation and wildlife or hikers above can dislodge rocks without warning.
Move well clear of steep talus aprons and undercut embankments onto broad, stable ground with unobstructed exits.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Reject unstable bluffs, talus aprons and rain-soaked slopes where falling rock or soil slumps threaten camp.
applies: Bluffs, canyons, rocky lake shores, road cuts and steep forested hillsides, especially during freeze-thaw cycles or heavy rain.
equipment: Daylight inspection vantage, map and headlamp for pre-dark checks.

failure.text: Tucked under an inviting cliff overhang for rain cover without noticing fresh chipped rock fragments and dripping fractured ledges overhead.

verify.text: Confirm zero fresh rockfall debris, overhanging loose stone or saturated slump scars upslope of the shelter and exit path.

stop.text: Reject any cliff overhang, boulder field base or visibly slumping hillside regardless of how well it blocks rain or wind.

diagram: Fractured bluff overhead | Fresh talus fall zone | Move to broad stable ground
visual: Environmental hillside cross-section mapping freeze-thaw rockfall paths, saturated root-slump zones and safe setback terrain. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Orient shelter entrances relative to prevailing wind and storm shifts
origin: NWS wind safety and B012 P10/P12; new manuscript

action.text: Observe cloud motion, tree sway, snow drift tails and forecast frontal passages to identify both current wind direction and expected overnight wind shifts.
Aim the lowest, narrowest or most reinforced side of the shelter into the expected wind and place the door on the leeward or crosswind side to limit blowing rain and drifting snow.
Avoid pitching an open tarp mouth directly into oncoming wind—open fronts act like parachutes that tear tie-outs and strip away trapped calm air.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Position low aerodynamic faces toward wind while protecting entrances from driven rain, snow drift and gusts.
applies: Pitching manufactured tents, tarps or emergency windbreaks in breezy, wet or winter conditions.
equipment: Weather forecast showing wind shift direction, shelter guyline kit and natural terrain wind cues.

failure.text: Facing a tent door into an approaching cold front because the sunset view faces west, flooding the vestibule and packing snow across the zipper.

verify.text: Confirm the windward profile is low and guyed cleanly while the doorway opens into calmer leeward air with a clear exit.

stop.text: If shifting gusts push against an exposed broad wall and threaten pole or anchor failure, re-orient before dark or move to a more sheltered site.

diagram: Wind hits narrow low profile | Door faces calmer leeward side | Watch for frontal wind shift
visual: Mechanism diagram illustrating airflow deflection over a low windward shelter face versus parachute uplift into an exposed door. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Separate cooking, food storage and sleeping areas in wildlife country
origin: USFS responsible recreation and NPS camping; new manuscript

action.text: Locate cooking, eating and dishwashing areas well downwind and separated from sleeping shelters according to local land-agency setback rules.
Store all food, trash, toiletries, lip balm and food-stained clothing in approved wildlife-resistant containers or lockers—never inside tents or sleeping bags.
Keep portable stoves strictly outdoors at the cooking area; cooking inside tents combines wildlife attraction with lethal carbon monoxide and burn hazards.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Keep food odors, cooking spills and scented supplies isolated from tents and sleeping gear.
applies: Backcountry and campground sites in bear, raccoon, rodent and wider wildlife habitats.
equipment: Agency-approved food storage (bear canister, food locker or permitted hang system), separate outdoor stove area and clean sealable odor bags.

failure.text: Snacking inside a sleeping bag or stashing wrappers and cooking pots in a tent vestibule overnight.

verify.text: Confirm sleeping shelters contain zero food, scented items or cooking equipment and that all attractants are secured per unit rules.

stop.text: If aggressive wildlife approaches camp or storage fails, follow local agency safety protocols, maintain safe distance and report to land managers.

diagram: Sleeping shelter odor-free | Downwind outdoor cook area | Approved wildlife storage

title: Choose between existing buildings, vehicles, tents and improvised cover
origin: Ready.gov shelter, NWS winter and B012 P02; new manuscript

action.text: Prefer a safely accessible substantial building first, or a safely parked enclosed hard-topped vehicle for lightning and winter storms when no building is reachable.
Use a purpose-made tent or tarp in its rated weather range only when safely sited clear of flood, lightning, tornado and hazard-tree risks.
Treat improvised natural windbreaks as a last-resort exposure measure when no manufactured shelter or safe refuge exists—never as an equivalent substitute for rated shelter.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prioritize proven engineered structures over fragile fabric tents or risky improvised builds during developing hazards.
applies: Any outdoor or travel disruption where multiple shelter options might be safely reachable.
equipment: Local map, weather alerts and realistic assessment of travel distance and visibility.

failure.text: Spending hours building a shaky branch hut while a trailhead vehicle or ranger shelter sits safely twenty minutes back along a verified road.

verify.text: Name the highest-grade shelter reachable via a verified safe route before committing effort to building or pitching cover.

stop.text: Never leave a safe building or stranded winter vehicle into blinding visibility or severe storm hazards just to try a different shelter.

diagram: Substantial building first | Safe vehicle or rated tent | Improvised windbreak last resort
visual: Decision tree ranking substantial buildings, safe vehicles, rated tents and improvised windbreaks by hazard protection and reachability. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Match shelter-in-place rooms to wind, tornado or outdoor air hazards
origin: Ready.gov shelter and NWS tornado safety; new manuscript

action.text: For tornadoes and extreme straight-line winds, move immediately to a basement, storm cellar or lowest-floor small interior room away from windows and exterior walls.
For outdoor chemical releases or heavy wildfire smoke, follow official orders to close windows, shut off HVAC/ventilation intakes and move to an interior room until officials issue an all-clear.
Never run portable generators, charcoal grills or unvented camp stoves inside a shelter-in-place room, basement or attached garage; keep CO alarms working and exits reachable.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Select the right interior room and preparation actions inside a building for distinct household emergencies.
applies: Homes, cabins and sturdy buildings during tornado warnings, high winds, winter storms or outdoor hazardous-material/smoke alerts.
equipment: Battery radio or alert phone, flashlights, sturdy shoes, drinking water and emergency kit.

failure.text: Sheltering near large windows during a tornado warning, or running an indoor camp stove inside a sealed smoke-protection room.

verify.text: Household members can name the exact room for wind/tornado versus air-quality alerts and confirm working exits and CO alarms.

stop.text: If structural damage, fire, rising floodwater or suspected carbon monoxide threatens the shelter room, evacuate immediately to safer ground per official guidance.

diagram: Tornado: lowest interior room | Smoke/hazmat: shut intakes | Never burn fuel indoors
visual: Comparative configuration contrasting tornado interior-core rooms, sealed outdoor-air refuge rooms and winter-storm shelter precautions. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Evaluate shoreline, wetland and floodplain setback before pitching
origin: NWS flood safety and NPS Leave No Trace; new manuscript

action.text: Pitch above high-water drift lines, gravel bars and floodplains—remembering upstream rain or dam releases can raise rivers hours later under clear local skies.
Maintain agency-required setbacks from lakeshores and streams to protect water quality, keep off saturated spongy soils that cannot hold tent stakes and reduce cold damp mist.
Inspect the bank for fresh mud lines, flattened grass or lodged woody debris that reveal recent flood heights, and verify an uphill dry escape route.

objective: Stay above rising water, wave surge, saturated soils and marsh instability near lakes, rivers and creeks.
applies: Camping near lakes, canoe routes, river bars, creek bends and Upper Midwest wetlands.
equipment: Topographic map, local water-level or dam-release alerts and durable shelter kit.

failure.text: Pitching on a flat scenic sandbar below a river cutbank that floods overnight from distant watershed storms.

verify.text: Confirm the tent pad sits above visible high-water marks, on firm draining soil, with an unobstructed uphill exit.

stop.text: Vacate shoreline or valley-bottom sites immediately if river levels rise, water turns suddenly muddy or a Flood Watch/Warning is issued.

title: Separate conductive, convective, radiative and evaporative heat loss
origin: NWS cold safety and CDC hypothermia; new manuscript

action.text: Block conduction into cold ground or snow first using dry uncompressed insulation beneath the body; air and ground drain heat rapidly through compressed fabric.
Block convection with a windbreak or windproof shell, and limit evaporation by shedding damp cotton, venting sweat during work and keeping rain off insulation.
Recognize that radiation still escapes to clear night skies and cold walls; overhead cover and dry lofted layers slow radiative cooling without sealing away fresh breathing air.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Target each distinct physical heat-loss pathway with the right barrier instead of relying on a single layer.
applies: Designing and troubleshooting cold-weather clothing, bedding and shelter systems in any environment.
equipment: Ground insulation pad, windproof outer barrier, dry insulating loft and vapor-management clothing layers.

failure.text: Wrapping in a windproof jacket while lying directly on frozen soil, or piling on thick wool while standing exposed in driving wind.

verify.text: Point to the exact barrier addressing ground contact, moving air, wetness and sky exposure in your current setup.

stop.text: If shivering becomes uncontrollable, speech slurs or hands fumble despite barriers, stop adjusting gear and initiate hypothermia escalation and emergency help.

diagram: Conduction -> ground pad | Convection -> wind barrier | Evaporation -> keep dry
visual: Mechanism diagram mapping conductive, convective, evaporative and radiative body heat-loss pathways to matched physical barriers. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Control interior condensation with airflow and rainfly clearance
origin: B012 P18 and NPS camping shelter guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Keep manufacturer-designed high and low vents open—even in cold weather—so warm moist breath escapes upward rather than condensing onto fabric and dripping onto bedding.
Guy out the rainfly cleanly so a continuous air gap separates the wet outer fly from the breathable inner tent wall; fabric touching fabric wicks water straight inside.
Keep wet boots, rain shells and packs out of dry sleeping spaces where practical, and wipe down interior frost or condensation gently before packing or shifting bags.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent exhaled water vapor and damp gear from soaking sleeping bags and frosting inner shelter walls.
applies: Occupied single-wall or double-wall tents, bivies and tarps in cool, humid or freezing weather.
equipment: Tent with functional upper and lower vents, rainfly guylines, absorbent cloth and dry storage bags.

failure.text: Zipping every tent vent completely shut in cold air to stay warm, turning the shelter interior into a dripping condensation chamber that wets sleeping loft.

verify.text: Confirm upper/lower vents remain clear, rainfly stands off the inner canopy and sleeping bags stay clear of damp wall edges.

stop.text: Never run a stove, candle or heater inside a tent to dry condensation; if wet bedding compromises warmth, replace with dry reserves or relocate to safer refuge.

diagram: Open high and low vents | Keep fly-to-inner air gap | Protect dry sleeping loft
visual: Cutaway view of a double-wall tent illustrating warm vapor airflow out upper vents, rainfly clearance gap and dry bedding separation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Layer groundsheets without funneling rainwater under the tent floor
origin: B012 P12 and NPS camping gear; new manuscript

action.text: Trim or fold the groundsheet cleanly underneath the shelter so every edge stops a few inches inside the tent floor perimeter—never sticking out past the rainfly drip line.
Place the groundsheet on smooth, cleared durable ground free of sharp sticks or stones that can puncture waterproof coatings under body weight.
Recognize that a waterproof groundsheet stops liquid seepage only—it provides almost no thermal insulation from cold ground, so an insulating pad is still mandatory inside.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect tent floors from abrasion and damp soil while preventing protruding plastic edges from collecting rain pools.
applies: Pitching a commercial tent or tarp shelter over damp soil, gravel or wet forest duff.
equipment: Purpose-sized tent footprint or clean groundsheet slightly smaller than the floor, plus dry sleeping pad.

failure.text: Spreading an oversized blue tarp out beyond the tent walls where it catches roof runoff and channels a puddle directly underneath the floor seams.

verify.text: Walk the perimeter and confirm zero groundsheet fabric protrudes beyond the shelter wall or catches roof drips.

stop.text: If surface water begins flowing across the pad despite proper groundsheet tucking, relocate the shelter to higher draining ground immediately.

diagram: Roof sheds outside drip line | Groundsheet tucked inside floor | Insulating pad above floor
visual: Cutaway cross-section showing properly tucked footprint inside the tent perimeter versus an oversized tarp channeling rain underneath. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Stack foam and inflatable pads for cold ground insulation
origin: B012 P11 and NPS winter camping; new manuscript

action.text: Combine a closed-cell foam pad underneath an insulated inflatable pad in cold conditions to increase ground separation and shield the air pad from punctures.
Inspect inflatable valves and seams before bedtime and avoid over-pressurizing or dragging air pads over pine cones, gravel or sharp frozen twigs.
Keep underbody insulation centered beneath shoulders, hips and torso—not just the head—using folded dry spare clothing or a dry pack under feet if a short pad is used.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Maintain reliable underbody thermal separation on frozen soil or snow and protect against inflatable-pad puncture failure.
applies: Cold-weather overnight stops, snow camping and chilly ground emergencies.
equipment: Closed-cell foam sleeping pad, insulated inflatable pad if carried, patch kit and dry ground barrier.

failure.text: Relying on a single uninsulated air mattress on frozen ground, where convective air movement inside the pad drains core warmth all night.

verify.text: Lie briefly in full sleep position to confirm no shoulder, hip or knee presses directly against cold ground or deflated chambers.

stop.text: If an inflatable pad fails in freezing weather and no dry foam or backup ground insulation keeps the sleeper warm, switch to dry natural/clothing buffers and reassess exit or rescue.

diagram: Sleeper and dry bag | Insulated pad layer | Closed-cell foam on cold ground
visual: Material cross-section stacking sleeping bag, insulated air pad, puncture-resistant closed-cell foam and frozen ground substrate. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Protect sleeping bags from loft compression and foot-box moisture
origin: B012 P04–P06 and NPS camping gear; new manuscript

action.text: Pack sleeping bags inside a sealed waterproof liner during travel so rain, river splashes or leaking water bottles cannot reach the insulation.
Change into dry sleep-only base layers and dry socks before entering the bag, and avoid tucking your nose and mouth inside the bag—exhaled breath condenses inside the loft overnight.
Keep the foot box and outer shell clear of damp tent walls and give sleeping bags time to loft fully after unpacking; compressed down or wet fibers lose thermal resistance rapidly.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Preserve trapped dead-air insulation inside synthetic or down sleeping systems throughout wet or multi-night trips.
applies: Overnight backcountry camping and cold-weather emergency delays using sleeping bags or quilts.
equipment: Waterproof pack liner or dry compression sack, dry dedicated sleep base layers and insulated sleeping pad.

failure.text: Breathing inside a cinched sleeping bag hood all night or stuffing a damp jacket into the foot box, saturating down insulation by morning.

verify.text: Confirm the bag stays inside dry storage during transit, lofts evenly at camp and remains clear of damp tent fabric and exhaled moisture.

stop.text: If down or primary insulation becomes saturated in cold weather and cannot be safely replaced with dry layers, abort overnight exposure and move to warm refuge or request help.

title: Use reflective emergency blankets and bivies while managing vapor buildup
origin: NPS Ten Essentials and NWS winter; new manuscript

action.text: Use an emergency reflective sheet primarily as a windproof outer shell or lean-to reflector over existing dry insulating layers and a ground barrier—thin foil alone conducts cold straight from the ground.
Keep the face unobstructed and leave a controlled neck or side opening on emergency bivy sacks so sweat and warm breath can escape rather than drenching your inner clothes.
Handle thin metalized film gently away from sharp twigs, rocks and open flames—standard mylar tears instantly from a small nick and melts near fire.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Deploy emergency reflective sheets or sacks effectively as wind and radiant barriers without creating hypothermia-inducing condensation.
applies: Unplanned cold stops, waiting for rescue or augmenting insulation during emergency delays.
equipment: Heavy-duty reflective emergency blanket or bivy sack, dry insulating layers and separate ground pad.

failure.text: Climbing inside a sealed plastic emergency bag in damp clothes directly on frozen earth, waking soaked in trapped sweat and chilled by ground conduction.

verify.text: Confirm dry insulation lies beneath and inside the reflective layer, breathing space is clear and edges are protected from tearing.

stop.text: Do not assume a pocket emergency blanket guarantees overnight winter survival; monitor companions for confusion or drowsiness and activate help early.

title: Avoid cotton and manage damp outer shells inside sleeping areas
origin: NWS winter, CDC hypothermia and B012 P05–P06; new manuscript

action.text: Leave cotton shirts, jeans and cotton socks out of cold/wet field kits—cotton absorbs water readily, collapses thermally and accelerates cooling against skin.
Shake snow and droplets off outer shells before entering shelter and isolate wet boots, rain jackets and wet gloves in a vestibule or waterproof bag apart from dry bedding.
Change out of damp daytime base layers only after entering wind-protected shelter with dry replacement garments immediately in hand.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Keep moisture-holding fabrics off skin and prevent wet outer rainwear or snow-dusted gear from soaking dry sleep insulation.

title: Adapt warm-weather tarp and shade pitch for solar heat and airflow
origin: CDC heat, NWS heat and Ready.gov heat guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Pitch an elevated open tarp or canopy high enough for unobstructed cross-breeze airflow beneath it, avoiding dark enclosed tents during midday sun.
Angle the shade canopy to track the sun's afternoon arc and orient the open sides to capture prevailing breeze rather than trapping stagnant hot air.
Pair shaded rest with reduced midday exertion, cool hydration and continuous group monitoring for heat exhaustion or heat stroke.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Reduce direct solar radiation while maximizing cross-breeze ventilation during hot or humid weather.
applies: Hot sunny camps, midday rest stops and heat-wave outdoor delays where enclosed tents overheat rapidly.
equipment: Light-colored or reflective tarp, trekking poles or legal attachment points, guylines and safe drinking water.

failure.text: Resting inside a zipped sun-baked tent during a 95°F afternoon, driving interior heat index far above ambient air temperature.

verify.text: Confirm full overhead shade across the rest area, steady air movement beneath the canopy and easy access to safe drinking water.

stop.text: If anyone develops confusion, slurred speech, collapse or stops coping with heat, call 911 and begin rapid cooling immediately.

title: Compare freestanding dome, tunnel and trekking-pole tent geometries
origin: NPS camping gear and NWS wind safety; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that freestanding dome tents hold basic shape without stakes for positioning on rock or hard pads, yet still MUST be staked and guyed against wind lift.
Recognize that tunnel and non-freestanding trekking-pole tents rely completely on opposing stake tension and guyline alignment to stand; one failed end stake can flatten the whole frame.
Follow the manufacturer's exact pole-sleeve, clip and guy-out sequence rather than substituting missing poles or skipping guy points in breezy weather.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Understand how pole architecture and stake dependence affect setup, stability and weather limits across manufactured tents.
applies: Selecting or pitching commercial tents across forest sites, rocky pads and windy open terrain.
equipment: Complete tent body, rainfly, matching poles, full stake set and manufacturer pitch instructions.

failure.text: Leaving a freestanding dome tent unstaked while stepping away, letting a sudden gust tumble or tear the shelter across camp.

verify.text: Confirm all pole tips seat fully in grommets, guylines tension evenly per instructions and the shelter stays firmly anchored when tested gently by hand.

stop.text: Do not use a three-season geometry in severe storms, heavy wet snow or high winds outside its manufacturer limits; relocate to substantial shelter.

title: Compare A-frame, lean-to and low-storm tarp pitch configurations
origin: B003 tarp plate and NPS shelter guidance; new manuscript

action.text: Use a symmetrical A-frame pitch for overhead rain protection with open end ventilation; drop edges closer to the ground when blowing rain enters from the sides.
Use an open lean-to pitch only for mild windbreak or shade when rain will not swirl under the high open front; expect wind shifts to expose the interior.
Use a low-profile storm pitch (half-pyramid or low windward wedge) with windward edge near the ground and leeward vent when gusts rise, accepting reduced headroom and keeping exits reachable.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Match tarp pitch geometry to shifting wind, rain angle and ventilation needs without overclaiming storm resistance.
applies: Commercial backcountry tarps pitched on permitted durable sites with dry ground insulation.
equipment: Rated tarp with reinforced tie-outs, clean cordage, stakes, trekking poles or lawful tree anchors and groundsheet.

failure.text: Pitching a flat high tarp in heavy rain, allowing water to pool in the center until fabric tears or tie-outs pull free.

verify.text: Confirm taut sloped runoff planes with zero water-pooling sags, clear exit clearance and reliable ground-splash setback.

stop.text: Tarps offer no lightning protection and limited defense against severe squalls, heavy snow or extreme wind; relocate to rated or substantial shelter when storms intensify.

title: Understand load paths across ridgepoles, tent poles, fabric and guylines
origin: B012 P13 and structural mechanics principles; new manuscript

action.text: Trace downward and sideways loads from the roof surface through poles or ridgelines into tensioned guylines and ground anchors—the weakest link in that chain governs failure.
Keep pole joints fully seated, fabric panels evenly taut without concentrated stress wrinkles and guylines angled outward to oppose wind lift cleanly.
Recognize that improvised deadfall frames and field-cut poles have unknown wood grain, rot and joint friction—never assign them unvalidated snow-load or wind-load capacities.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Trace how wind, fabric tension and precipitation forces travel through a shelter frame down to ground anchors.
applies: Inspecting manufactured tents, tarps and emergency windbreaks before and during weather exposure.
equipment: Complete shelter assembly and inspection checklist (no unvalidated field load testing).

failure.text: Attaching a heavy tarp mid-panel with a pebble knot or leaning snow-laden branches onto a cracked deadwood ridgepole.

verify.text: Confirm every load-bearing junction—pole ferrule, corner seam, guyline knot and ground stake—shows even tension without kinks, splits or loose play.

stop.text: Any bent pole, splitting wood support, tearing seam or slipping anchor interrupts the load path; unload and vacate the shelter rather than sleeping beneath it.

title: Inspect fabric coatings, seam tape, zippers and pole joints before use
origin: NPS camping gear and Ready.gov kit maintenance; new manuscript

action.text: Pitch or lay out the shelter in daylight to inspect pole ferrules for hairline splits, check internal shock-cord elasticity and confirm all rainfly buckles and tie-outs are intact.
Check interior waterproof coatings and seam tape for stickiness, flaking, mildew odor or pinholes, and slide every door zipper gently to verify clean teeth alignment.
Pack a compatible pole repair splint, fabric patch tape and spare guyline cord matched to the shelter before departure.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Catch worn waterproofing, cracked shock-cord, bent ferrules and snagged zippers before field weather exposes them.
applies: Pre-trip inspection of stored tents, tarps, bivies and repair kits at home or before storm seasons.
equipment: Shelter set, spare pole splint sleeve, seam-safe repair tape, spare cordage and clean dry test space.

failure.text: Discovering peeling polyurethane floor coating and snapped pole shock-cord at dusk during a cold downpour.

verify.text: Confirm complete component count (body, fly, poles, stakes, guys, repair kit) and smooth zipper/pole operation prior to packing.

stop.text: Do not rely on a shelter with split pole ferrules, failed floor waterproofing or broken door zippers for wet or cold overnight travel.

title: Match stakes and anchors to soil, sand, mud and compacted snow limits
origin: NPS camping and NWS wind safety; new manuscript

action.text: Check substrate firmness before pitching; slim wire pegs pull straight out of soft mud, loose sand, thick leaf duff and dry snow under modest wind gusts.
Drive stakes at an outward angle per shelter instructions into firm soil, or use wide snow/sand stakes or clean wrapped deadman rocks/logs where terrain rules allow—avoiding live roots.
Test anchor firmness gently by hand before relying on the pitch and recheck anchors after rain saturates the soil or afternoon sun softens snowpack.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize how substrate type changes anchor holding behavior without assuming unvalidated pullout capacities.
applies: Anchoring manufactured tents and tarps on forest soil, rocky pads, wet mud, sand or consolidated snow.
equipment: Stakes matched to expected ground (Y/V-profile stakes, wider sand/snow stakes or clean deadman/rock options where lawful).

failure.text: Expecting standard aluminum wire pegs pushed into wet forest duff or melting spring snow to hold a tarp through a night squall.

verify.text: Confirm every primary corner and windward guyline sits in firm substrate and resists steady hand tension without creeping.

stop.text: Anchor strength varies wildly with soil moisture and snow crystal state—no universal pullout rating is implied; relocate to protected refuge if anchors creep in rising wind.

title: Distribute tension across guylines without overloading corners or tie-outs
origin: NPS camping and NWS wind safety; new manuscript

action.text: Attach guylines strictly to manufacturer-reinforced seam loops and pole-crossing tabs—never pinch unreinforced fabric panels that tear under gust loads.
Set guyline angles cleanly outward along seam load lines and equalize tension across opposing sides so no single windward corner takes the full shock load.
Use high-visibility cordage or mark lines clearly at walking routes so companions do not trip in the dark, snapping stakes or ripping seams.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Share wind loads across multiple reinforced attachment points rather than stressing a single fabric corner.
applies: Securing tents and tarps in open, breezy or storm-prone camps using manufacturer tie-out loops.
equipment: High-visibility reflective guyline cord, line tensioners or adjustable hitches and suitable stakes.

failure.text: Guying out only one windward corner tightly while leaving pole-midpoints unguyed, snapping a flexed tent pole during a cross-gust.

verify.text: Walk around the shelter checking that all windward guylines share even tension, stay clear of exit paths and keep rainfly separated from inner walls.

stop.text: If gusts cause fabric seams to stretch noticeably or lines repeatedly slacken, lower exposure or move immediately to substantial shelter.

diagram: Reinforced seam loops | Even outward tension angles | Visible lines clear of exits
visual: Exploded layout showing reinforced guyline attachment points, balanced opposing tension vectors and unobstructed walking/exit corridors. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Recognize material strength limits of coated nylon, polyester and plastic sheeting
origin: NPS camping gear and fire safety; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that silicone- or polyurethane-coated nylon sags when wet and requires re-tensioning in rain, whereas polyester stretches less when wet but varies by denier and coating quality.
Recognize that disposable polyethylene sheeting tears rapidly along small punctures, traps heavy condensation and offers low wind resistance compared to ripstop fabrics.
Keep ALL synthetic fabrics and plastic sheets well away from stove flames, campfire sparks and hot coals—ultralight synthetics melt and ignite rapidly, causing severe burns.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Account for wet stretch, UV degradation, tear propagation and heat/spark vulnerability across common shelter fabrics.
applies: Selecting, pitching and caring for manufactured tarps, tents and improvised plastic sheeting.
equipment: Shelter material specification sheet, compatible repair tape and fire-separation awareness.

failure.text: Pitching a nylon rainfly tightly in dry afternoon air without re-checking wet sag at night, letting wet fabric droop onto sleeping bags, or sparking a synthetic tarp near a stove.

verify.text: Identify your shelter's primary fabric class, check wet-tension adjustment access and confirm zero flame or spark sources operate nearby.

stop.text: Retire UV-brittle, tearing or delaminated shelter fabric before storms; never patch over failed structural seams to push a shelter into severe weather.

diagram: Nylon: retension when wet | Polyester: lower wet sag | All synthetics: melt near flame
visual: Comparative configuration contrasting wet-stretch, tear behavior, UV aging and spark/heat sensitivity across nylon, polyester and plastic film. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Evaluate natural windbreak barriers without adding overhead branch loads
origin: B012 P10 and NWS winter safety; new manuscript

action.text: Select an immovable natural barrier—such as a terrain rise, solid rock outcrop or firmly embedded low log—after confirming zero overhead dead limbs, rolling rocks or runoff channels.
Position your dry insulated bed tightly on the calmer leeward side while keeping an open, unobstructed exit path clear of stacked sticks or snow banks.
Resist stacking heavy dead branches overhead to create a roof; a low open windbreak paired with dry insulation avoids overhead collapse hazards and saves critical energy.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Use sound natural terrain features or low fallen logs for wind shelter while keeping overhead collapse risk zero.
applies: Emergency exposure reduction on stable ground when no manufactured shelter or building is available.
equipment: Existing stable natural feature (terrain rise, sound boulder or immovable grounded log), dry insulation and wind clothing.

failure.text: Wedging beneath an unstable tilted root-ball or piling heavy rotten limbs across a log where wind or snow can collapse them onto the sleeper.

verify.text: Confirm the natural barrier cannot roll or shift, zero load hangs overhead and you can stand and exit freely.

stop.text: If wind shifts around the barrier, blowing snow buries the bed or exposure worsens, relocate to a safer refuge or summon emergency help.

diagram: Stable grounded barrier | Dry bed in leeward eddy | Zero overhead load; clear exit

title: Understand structural hazards of improvised debris roofs and A-frames
origin: B012 P13 natural winter A-frame; adapted historical material

action.text: Inspect site safety first—reject dead standing trees, runoff channels and snow-loaded canopies before considering any natural materials.
Recognize that deadfall ridgepoles and side ribs have unpredictable internal rot, knots and joint slippage; fallen-branch framing carries ZERO validated snow-load or wind-load rating.
Recognize that wet leaves, damp moss or melting snow piled onto an improvised frame soak bedding rapidly and add sudden roof weight that can collapse onto an occupied sleeping area.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize why fallen-branch A-frames and debris huts lack verified load ratings and when to reject overhead builds.
applies: Conceptual assessment of improvised emergency shelters; this card is NOT a snow-load build specification.
equipment: Safe terrain assessment; if equipped, prefer a purpose-made shelter or existing safe refuge over improvised wood framing.

failure.text: Sleeping beneath a heavy debris roof built from brittle deadwood during wet snowfall or rising wind.

verify.text: Confirm you can explain why a low windbreak plus dry ground insulation beats an untested overhead roof when wood soundness or weather loading is uncertain.

stop.text: Never occupy an improvised roof that sags, creaks, shifts or accumulates snow; move immediately to clear ground, maintain wind/ground protection and seek help.

visual: Cutaway hazard schematic of an improvised branch A-frame labeling unvalidated ridge support, wet debris weight and collapse risk. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Understand lean-to airflow and unvalidated fire-separation boundaries
origin: B012 P14 lean-to and fire separation; adapted historical material

action.text: Treat an open lean-to strictly as a directional windbreak clear of overhead hazards and runoff, keeping an unobstructed exit at all times.
Treat any outdoor fire as an independent hazard requiring current burn permission, wind screening, water ready and a named awake attendant—never sleep next to an unattended fire.
Recognize there is NO universally safe fire-to-shelter clearance distance: wind eddies, dry brush, synthetic fabric melting, sparks and radiant heat vary at every site.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Separate open windbreak function from outdoor campfire hazards without assuming any universal safe clearance distance.
applies: Conceptual shelter-and-fire relationship; open fires require lawful authorization, weather checks and constant attendance.
equipment: Safe site assessment, dry insulation layers, and—only where fire is lawful and controllable—water and stirring tool.

failure.text: Building a roaring fire close to a synthetic tarp or dry brush lean-to using a memorized step-count clearance and falling asleep while wind shifts sparks onto bedding.

verify.text: Confirm exposure control relies on dry insulation and wind protection first, with zero flame or hot embers threatening fabric, wood or breathing air.

stop.text: Extinguish or relocate an outdoor fire immediately if smoke enters the shelter, wind shifts toward dry materials or radiant heat warms shelter surfaces; never burn fuel inside an enclosure.

visual: Cutaway schematic highlighting swirling wind/spark hazard between an open lean-to and an outdoor fire, explicitly noting no universal safe distance. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Recognize why snow trenches require training, tools and roof-stability checks
origin: B012 P15 snow trench; adapted historical material

action.text: Prefer existing stable buildings, safe vehicles or rated tents over digging snow when exposure, wind or fatigue is rising—digging burns heavy energy and causes dangerous sweating.
Exclude avalanche slopes, cornices, stream channels and unstable granular snow; snow depth alone NEVER proves roof strength or block cohesion.
Without proper snow tools, formal training and an unobstructed escape plan, never roof over an excavated trench; use a low open windwall and insulated bed or existing refuge instead.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Understand the collapse, drift-burial and exhaustion hazards of excavated snow trenches before attempting any digging.
applies: Winter snowpack environments; this card states hazard boundaries and is NOT an untrained construction specification.
equipment: Formal winter training, avalanche check, snow shovel, dry reserve layers and rescue communication plan.

failure.text: Digging a roofed snow trench with bare gloves in sugary unconsolidated snow, soaking clothing with sweat and risking sudden slab collapse.

verify.text: Confirm avalanche terrain is excluded, dry layers stay protected from sweat and no occupant sleeps beneath an unverified snow roof.

stop.text: Cracking, settling, dripping thaw, blocked drift exits or advancing hypothermia requires vacating any snow excavation immediately and moving to safer surface cover or rescue.

title: Recognize why snow caves and quinzhees carry collapse and air hazards
origin: B012 P16 snow cave / quinzhee; adapted historical material

action.text: Treat snow caves and quinzhees as structural systems requiring specialized training, proper snow sintering evaluation and supervised practice—never as a no-gear emergency shortcut.

Recognize four acute hazards inside snow enclosures: unverified ceiling collapse (especially during warming or rain-on-snow), blocked ventilation holes, snow-drifted exits and rapid lethal CO from any stove or candle.
Exclude avalanche runouts, steep snow drifts and cornices entirely; keep digging tools inside with occupants only under trained protocols and maintain continuous external visibility/markers.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Identify fatal collapse, suffocation, drifting-exit and carbon monoxide boundaries that make excavated snow caves advanced-only.
applies: Deep-snow backcountry zones; strictly an informational hazard boundary, NOT an approved improvised survival procedure.
equipment: Qualified winter instructor supervision, avalanche evaluation, dedicated shovels, snow probe/markers and CO-free heat rules.

failure.text: Attempting an unsupervised quinzhee in wet warming snow or lighting a small camp stove inside a snow cave to warm the air.

verify.text: Confirm that without qualified training and suitable snowpack, the group chooses existing refuge, rated winter tent or surface windbreak and rescue signaling instead.

stop.text: Ceiling sag, cracking sounds, stuffy air, drowsiness, headache or drifting exit blockage demands immediate exit to fresh air and safer shelter.
